tier_reason: The README gives the 19.3 MB (Bloom filter cascade, 2024-08-29) vs 8.5 MB (clubcard) comparison and states the 56% reduction itself. The linked peer-reviewed paper (Schanck, IEEE S&P 2025, DOI 10.1109/sp61157.2025.00128) reports issuer-partitioned clubcards that are on average 54% smaller than Bloom filter cascades for the same late-2024 CRLite data (Figure 1). That peer-reviewed evidence of the win against the baseline justifies upgrading from C to B; it is a size result with no timing methodology, so it cannot be A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: 8.5 MB (clubcard) vs 19.3 MB (Mozilla's CRLite Bloom filter cascade published 2024-08-29), which the README states as a 56% reduction in size. The IEEE S&P 2025 paper reports issuer-partitioned clubcards that are on average 54% smaller than Bloom filter cascades for the same data (2024-10-29 to 2024-11-11 snapshots).
corrections.stars_or_usage: 24 stars; clubcard-based CRLite has been the default revocation mechanism for all Firefox desktop users since Firefox 137 (Mozilla Hacks, Aug 2025) and is generated by Mozilla's CRLite backend
corrections.caveats: This is a memory/size comparison from production snapshots, not a timing benchmark, so no CPU or compiler details apply. The baseline is Mozilla's own prior multi-level Bloom-cascade encoding of the same dataset, not a generic third-party Bloom filter. Part of the gain comes from partitioning revocations by issuer rather than from Ribbon versus Bloom: the README estimates an issuer-sharded Bloom cascade would be about 13 MB. The README warns that the API and serialization format are not stable. Peer-reviewed paper: Schanck, 'Clubcards for the WebPKI', IEEE S&P 2025.

notes: The numbers are verbatim on the README, and the 56% is stated there, so it is not derived. The tier is upgraded to B via the IEEE S&P 2025 paper, which reports an average 54% size reduction vs Bloom cascades. Deployment is confirmed by the Mozilla Hacks post (CRLite enabled for all Firefox desktop users in Firefox 137). All metadata checks out (MPL-2.0, last commit 2026-07-31, 24 stars, not a fork or archived).

tier_reason: The README results table compares DCF against a Dynamic Bloom Filter implementation that ships in the repo (src_DBF/, makefile_DBF) on an i5-2430M. However, both makefiles compile with 'g++ -Wall' and no optimization flag (default -O0), so the -O0 baseline cap applies and the tier stays C, even though the design is also published at ICNP 2017.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Space: 2.5 MB (DCF) vs 10.8754 MB (DBF), labelled 4X. Time for 1M items: insert 1.08 s vs 1.69 s (1.5X), query 1.05 s vs 1.92 s (1.8X), delete 1.36 s vs 3.35 s (2.4X). Numbers and ratio labels are verbatim from the README results table; the README text summarizes this as 30-80% faster insert/query/delete and a 75% memory reduction.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: g++ -Wall with no -O flag (default -O0), for both DCF (makefile) and DBF (makefile_DBF); compiler version not stated
corrections.caveats: The baseline is a Dynamic Bloom Filter (a Bloom variant, implemented in the repo under src_DBF/), not the plain incumbent Bloom filter, so baseline_in_list=false. Both DCF and DBF are built by the repo makefiles without optimization (g++ -Wall, default -O0), so absolute times and ratios may not hold at -O2/-O3. Hardware is a 2011-era laptop CPU (i5-2430M). The repo has been unmaintained since 2017. Paper: Chen, Liao, Jin, Wu, 'The Dynamic Cuckoo Filter', ICNP 2017, DOI 10.1109/icnp.2017.8117563.

notes: The numbers match the README table; the only fix is DBF space_cost, which is 10.8754 MB (the record rounded it to 10.9). Both builds are unoptimized, which caps the tier at C despite the peer-reviewed ICNP 2017 paper. All metadata is correct (Apache-2.0, last commit 2017-11-16, 38 stars, abandoned).

tier_reason: The README only states 'compared to existing designs, E2CF reduces the query and insertion time by up to 82% and 28%', with no results table and no named baseline. The repo's test.cpp benchmarks only E2CF, includes no baseline code, and is built at -O0 (makefile: -std=c++0x -Wall). The NPC 2020 paper abstract (LNCS, DOI 10.1007/978-3-030-79478-1_32) repeats 82%/28% vs unnamed 'state-of-the-art designs', but the paywalled evaluation could not be checked, so the tier stays C.

corrections.baseline: State-of-the-art dynamic approximate-membership filters with filter-level extension (the paper's references suggest Dynamic Cuckoo Filter / Dynamic Bloom Filter; exact baselines are not named on the README or in the abstract)
corrections.claimed_speedup: Reduces query time by up to 82% and insertion time by up to 28% compared to existing designs (README; the NPC 2020 paper abstract says 82% and 28% vs 'state-of-the-art designs'). No raw numbers are published.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: /usr/bin/g++ -std=c++0x -Wall with no -O flag (default -O0), per makefile; compiler version not stated
corrections.caveats: The README does not name the baseline. The paper abstract says the comparison is against existing dynamic (filter-level-extensible) structures, not the static cuckoo filter, and its references include DCF (ICNP 2017) and DBF (TKDE 2010). The repo contains no baseline implementation or comparison harness; the committed result/result.txt holds uninitialized garbage values. The makefile builds without optimization. The hardware line gives no CPU model (Intel 2.60GHz, 64 GB RAM, RHEL 6.2). Paper: Yu, Wu, Chen, Jin, 'The Entry-Extensible Cuckoo Filter', NPC 2020, LNCS 12639 (2021).

notes: The 82%/28% claim appears verbatim on the README, but it is a bare percentage vs unnamed 'existing designs'. The paper abstract shows the baselines are dynamic filters, not the plain cuckoo filter, so I corrected baseline and set baseline_in_list=false. Metadata is correct (Apache-2.0, last commit 2020-08-29, 3 stars, abandoned).
